lessonTitle: Acute Coronary Syndromes: STEMI, NSTEMI and Unstable Angina

blocks.text: A 63-year-old publican collapses behind his bar with crushing central chest pressure, sweating and grey skin. The paramedic's 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. The next 90 minutes decide how much of his inferior wall of heart muscle survives, which is why the saying 'time is muscle' guides everything in this unit.

blocks.markdown:
**Mechanism first.** Most acute coronary syndromes (ACS) begin when an atherosclerotic plaque in an epicardial coronary artery ruptures or erodes. Exposed lipid core and collagen activate platelets and the coagulation cascade, and a thrombus forms on the plaque. What happens next depends on how completely and how persistently the thrombus blocks flow:

- **Complete, persistent occlusion** causes transmural ischaemia and necrosis spreading from endocardium to epicardium, producing **ST-segment elevation** on the ECG (STEMI).
- **Partial or intermittent occlusion** causes subendocardial ischaemia, producing ST depression or T-wave inversion, or a normal ECG (NSTEMI or unstable angina).

Myocyte death releases **cardiac troponin** (troponin I or T, structural proteins specific to heart muscle) into the blood. Troponin is therefore the biochemical marker that separates infarction from ischaemia without necrosis.

blocks.title: Acute coronary syndrome
blocks.text: ACS is the umbrella term for acute myocardial ischaemia due to coronary thrombosis. STEMI = ischaemic symptoms plus persistent ST elevation (or new left bundle branch block with a compatible history) and a rise and fall of troponin. NSTEMI = ischaemic symptoms, no persistent ST elevation, troponin raised above the 99th percentile upper reference limit with a rise and/or fall. Unstable angina = ischaemic symptoms at rest or with minimal exertion (or of new onset or crescendo pattern) with no troponin rise.

blocks.caption: Distinguishing the three ACS diagnoses. Troponin thresholds vary by assay and laboratory.
rows: ST elevation in two or more contiguous leads
ST depression, T inversion or normal
ST depression, T inversion or normal
Raised (but do not wait for it)

blocks.markdown: **Using troponin well.** Troponin starts to rise within a few hours of myocyte injury, so a single early sample can be normal. High-sensitivity assays are therefore repeated at a time interval set by local protocol (commonly at presentation and 1 to 3 hours later, or 3 to 6 hours after symptom onset). A rising or falling pattern supports acute myocardial injury; a persistently flat, mildly raised value suggests chronic injury (for example chronic kidney disease). Raised troponin is not specific to ACS: myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, sepsis and tachyarrhythmia can all raise it. **A STEMI is diagnosed from the clinical story and the ECG; reperfusion is never delayed to wait for a troponin result.**

blocks.title: Classifying a presentation
blocks.prompt: A 55-year-old man has 25 minutes of central chest tightness at rest, now settled. His ECG shows 1.5 mm horizontal ST depression in V4 to V6. High-sensitivity troponin is below the 99th percentile at presentation and at the repeat sample taken three hours later. Which ACS diagnosis applies?

steps.text: Ischaemic-sounding pain at rest means this is an ACS-type presentation, not stable exertional angina.
There is no persistent ST elevation, so this is not STEMI. The ST depression suggests subendocardial ischaemia.
Troponin was serially measured at the appropriate interval and stayed below the 99th percentile, so there is no evidence of myocyte necrosis.
Ischaemic symptoms and ECG change without troponin rise define unstable angina. He still needs antithrombotic therapy and risk stratification, because this lesion may progress to infarction.

blocks.answer: Unstable angina (not NSTEMI, because troponin did not rise).

blocks.markdown:
**Principles of early reperfusion.** In STEMI the goal is to open the artery as fast as possible. Two strategies exist:

- **Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI):** catheter-based angioplasty and stenting. It is the preferred option when it can be delivered quickly enough. UK practice offers primary PCI to people presenting within 12 hours of symptom onset when it can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given.
- **Fibrinolysis** (for example tenecteplase): a drug that activates plasminogen and dissolves fibrin. It is used when PCI cannot be delivered within that window, and is most effective given early. It is contraindicated by active bleeding, previous haemorrhagic stroke or other recent intracranial or major bleeding risks.

In NSTEMI and unstable angina there is no emergency reperfusion; angiography is timed by risk (immediate if unstable, otherwise within about 72 hours in UK practice).

items: Aspirin: loading dose (for example 300 mg orally, teaching example) as soon as ACS is suspected, then daily.
Second antiplatelet (P2Y12 inhibitor): ticagrelor or prasugrel with PCI; clopidogrel is used when the patient is on an oral anticoagulant or with fibrinolysis.
Parenteral anticoagulant: unfractionated heparin during PCI; fondaparinux in NSTEMI managed conservatively.
Analgesia and symptom relief: sublingual GTN, and an opioid for severe pain used cautiously. Oxygen only if saturation is below 94% on air.
Early secondary prevention: high-intensity statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor (especially with LV dysfunction), cardiac rehabilitation.

blocks.caption: Antithrombotic drug classes and how they work (doses are teaching examples only).
rows: Irreversibly blocks COX-1, lowering platelet thromboxane A2
Blocks the platelet ADP receptor P2Y12, reducing activation and aggregation
Potentiate antithrombin, inhibiting factor Xa (and thrombin for heparin)
Converts plasminogen to plasmin, which dissolves fibrin

blocks.title: Mean arterial pressure and the time budget
blocks.prompt: A 69-year-old woman with an anterior STEMI has BP 82/54 mmHg. She is at a hospital without PCI. Estimated ambulance transfer is 60 minutes and door-to-balloon at the PCI centre is 35 minutes. What is her mean arterial pressure (MAP), and does primary PCI meet the 120-minute rule?

steps.text: Use MAP as diastolic pressure plus one third of pulse pressure, with pulse pressure = systolic minus diastolic.
Pulse pressure is 82 - 54 = 28 mmHg, so MAP = 54 + 28/3 = 54 + 9.3 = 63.3 mmHg.
Estimated time to PCI is transfer plus door-to-balloon: 60 + 35 = 95 minutes, which is inside the 120-minute limit (margin 25 minutes).
Low blood pressure in anterior STEMI raises concern about cardiogenic shock, which strengthens the case for urgent PCI.

blocks.answer: MAP is about 63 mmHg and the predicted 95 minutes meets the 120-minute rule, so transfer for primary PCI.

blocks.markdown:
**Early complications of MI** are best remembered by mechanism:

1. **Electrical:** ventricular fibrillation (most common cause of death in the first hours), ventricular tachycardia, and bradyarrhythmias including AV block (common in inferior MI because the AV node is usually supplied by the right coronary artery).
2. **Pump failure:** left ventricular failure with pulmonary oedema and, when more than about 40% of the myocardium is lost, cardiogenic shock.
3. **Mechanical (typically days 3 to 7):** papillary muscle rupture (acute severe mitral regurgitation), ventricular septal rupture (new loud pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge) and free wall rupture (tamponade and sudden collapse).
4. **Inflammatory:** early pericarditis, with Dressler syndrome (post-MI pericarditis) occurring weeks later.

blocks.caption: Complication, clue and first-line response.
rows: Cardiac arrest protocol with immediate defibrillation
Atropine if unstable; temporary pacing if no response
Urgent revascularisation, critical-care support, inotropes as required
New harsh pansystolic murmur and thrill, sudden deterioration
Echocardiography, haemodynamic support, urgent surgical or device closure
Acute pulmonary oedema, new apical pansystolic murmur
Echocardiography, vasodilators and support, urgent surgery
Pleuritic pain relieved by sitting forward, rub
Simple analgesia; avoid high-dose NSAIDs early after MI

blocks.title: Do not wait for troponin in STEMI
blocks.text: Ischaemic symptoms with ST elevation in two contiguous leads mean STEMI. Delaying reperfusion to await troponin results costs myocardium. Conversely, a normal first troponin does not exclude an NSTEMI, so repeat it.

points: STEMI = persistent ST elevation from complete occlusion; NSTEMI = troponin rise without ST elevation; unstable angina = ischaemic symptoms without troponin rise.
Troponin needs serial sampling; the first value can be normal, and rises also occur in non-coronary conditions.
STEMI needs immediate reperfusion: primary PCI if deliverable within the 120-minute window, otherwise fibrinolysis, plus aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor and parenteral anticoagulation.
Early complications are electrical (VF, heart block), pump failure, mechanical (papillary muscle, septal or free wall rupture) and inflammatory (pericarditis).

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has 40 minutes of chest pressure. Her ECG shows ST depression and T-wave inversion in V4 to V6 with no ST elevation. High-sensitivity troponin rises from 9 ng/L at presentation to 210 ng/L at the repeat sample (99th percentile 14 ng/L). What is the diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Unstable angina has no troponin rise; here troponin clearly rose above the 99th percentile.
distractorRationale.b: STEMI requires persistent ST elevation, which is absent.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: ischaemic symptoms, no ST elevation and a troponin rise and above-threshold value indicate NSTEMI.
distractorRationale.d: Stable angina is exertional, predictable and does not cause troponin elevation.

questions.explanation: NSTEMI is defined by myocardial necrosis (rise of troponin above the 99th percentile) without persistent ST elevation. The ST depression indicates subendocardial ischaemia, and the troponin rise separates this from unstable angina.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with diabetes has had three episodes of rest chest pain over 24 hours, each lasting 10 minutes. He is now pain-free. ECG is normal. High-sensitivity troponin is below the 99th percentile on two samples taken at the interval set by the local protocol. Which is the best description?

options.text: Non-cardiac chest pain, no further assessment needed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: crescendo rest ischaemic pain with no troponin rise is unstable angina.
distractorRationale.b: NSTEMI needs a troponin rise, which did not occur.
distractorRationale.c: STEMI needs ST elevation on the ECG, which is absent.
distractorRationale.d: Recurrent rest pain in a diabetic patient is high-risk and needs risk stratification, not dismissal.

questions.explanation: Unstable angina is a clinical diagnosis of ischaemic symptoms at rest or in a crescendo pattern without troponin rise. It still carries a risk of progression to infarction, so antithrombotic therapy and risk stratification (with angiography as indicated) are required.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has an inferior STEMI with symptom onset 90 minutes ago. The nearest PCI centre cannot deliver PCI within the 120-minute window. Which feature in his history would be an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis?

distractorRationale.a: A previous MI is not a contraindication to fibrinolysis.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: prior haemorrhagic stroke carries a prohibitive risk of intracranial bleeding.
distractorRationale.c: Moderately raised BP is not an absolute contraindication (severe uncontrolled hypertension is a concern).
distractorRationale.d: Age alone is not a contraindication; older patients are often treated.

questions.explanation: Fibrinolytics dissolve fibrin in all clots, so history of haemorrhagic stroke or other intracranial or major bleeding risk makes the risk of life-threatening bleeding outweigh the benefit. Age and previous MI do not prevent fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism by which aspirin reduces thrombosis in ACS?

options.text: Blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor
Irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1, reducing thromboxane A2 production
Potentiates antithrombin to inhibit factor Xa

questions.correctOptionText: Irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1, reducing thromboxane A2 production

distractorRationale.a: This is the mechanism of ticagrelor, prasugrel and clopidogrel.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: platelets cannot make new COX-1, so the effect lasts the platelet lifespan.
distractorRationale.c: This describes fibrinolytics such as tenecteplase.

questions.explanation: Aspirin acetylates COX-1 irreversibly, lowering thromboxane A2 and so platelet activation and aggregation. Because platelets lack a nucleus they cannot regenerate the enzyme, so the effect persists for the platelet lifespan.

questions.stem: On day 4 after an inferior MI, a 74-year-old man develops sudden hypotension and breathlessness. A new harsh pansystolic murmur is heard loudest at the left lower sternal edge with a palpable thrill. Which complication is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Dressler syndrome presents weeks later with pleuritic pain and fever, not a murmur.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: new pansystolic murmur and thrill at the left sternal edge with haemodynamic collapse, a few days after MI.
distractorRationale.c: Pericarditis causes a friction rub, not a pansystolic murmur and shock.
distractorRationale.d: Free wall rupture gives tamponade and sudden collapse without a loud murmur.

questions.explanation: Septal rupture creates a left-to-right shunt across the infarcted septum, producing a loud pansystolic murmur and a thrill at the left sternal edge, typically 3 to 7 days after infarction. Echocardiography confirms it, and management is haemodynamic support and urgent repair.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old man on day 1 after an anterior MI is cold and clammy with BP 78/50 mmHg. Calculate his mean arterial pressure in mmHg using MAP = diastolic + one third of pulse pressure. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure is 78 - 50 = 28 mmHg. MAP = 50 + 28/3 = 50 + 9.3 = 59.3 mmHg, about 59 mmHg, which is below the roughly 65 mmHg target used in shock and supports a diagnosis of cardiogenic shock needing urgent revascularisation and critical-care support.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with STEMI presents 3 hours after symptom onset to a hospital without PCI. Ambulance transfer to the PCI centre takes 75 minutes and door-to-balloon time there is 40 minutes. The limit for choosing primary PCI over fibrinolysis is 120 minutes. By how many minutes does the predicted time to PCI fall inside (positive) or outside (negative) this limit? Give the margin in minutes.
questions.explanation: Predicted delay to PCI is transfer plus door-to-balloon, 75 + 40 = 115 minutes. The margin from the 120-minute limit is 120 - 115 = +5 minutes, so PCI is just deliverable and is preferred, although the margin is thin and any additional delay would shift the decision to fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: Explain why the diagnosis of STEMI must not wait for a troponin result, and why a single normal troponin taken early after symptom onset does not exclude NSTEMI. Describe how you would use serial troponin and the ECG to distinguish STEMI, NSTEMI and unstable angina.
markingGuide: STEMI is diagnosed from symptoms plus ST elevation in contiguous leads; complete occlusion needs immediate reperfusion
Delay to reperfusion causes irreversible myocardial loss ('time is muscle')
Troponin rises hours after necrosis starts, so an early sample may be normal
Repeat troponin at protocol interval; rise and/or fall above the 99th percentile indicates necrosis
NSTEMI: no ST elevation, troponin raised; unstable angina: no ST elevation, troponin not raised
Troponin is not specific for ACS (for example renal disease, sepsis, pulmonary embolism)
questions.explanation: The ECG, not the troponin, identifies the patient who needs immediate reperfusion, because ST elevation reflects persistent occlusion. Troponin is a marker of necrosis that lags behind ischaemia, so it must be repeated to separate NSTEMI from unstable angina and to avoid being misled by an early normal result.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man arrives at a PCI centre 80 minutes after the onset of crushing chest pain, with ST elevation in V1 to V4. Outline the immediate antithrombotic and reperfusion management and justify each component.
markingGuide: Aspirin loading dose to inhibit platelet COX-1
P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel; clopidogrel if on oral anticoagulant) for added platelet inhibition
Parenteral anticoagulant, for example unfractionated heparin during PCI
Primary PCI as the preferred reperfusion strategy when within the time window
Fibrinolysis is the alternative if PCI cannot be delivered within the window, after checking contraindications
Analgesia (GTN, cautious opioid), oxygen only if saturation below 94%, monitoring for arrhythmia
questions.explanation: Platelet-rich arterial thrombus is treated with dual antiplatelet therapy and an anticoagulant to limit propagation while mechanical reperfusion reopens the vessel. Primary PCI is preferred because it opens the artery more reliably and carries lower intracranial bleeding risk than fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is 36 hours into an inferior STEMI managed with PCI. She becomes light-headed with a heart rate of 32 beats per minute and BP 80/50 mmHg. The ECG shows P waves and QRS complexes occurring independently of each other. Identify the rhythm, explain why it is common in this infarct territory, and outline the management.
markingGuide: Complete (third-degree) AV block with AV dissociation
Right coronary artery usually supplies the AV node, so inferior MI causes nodal ischaemia
Often transient and may resolve with reperfusion and time
Haemodynamically unstable bradycardia: atropine first line
Temporary transvenous or transcutaneous pacing if atropine fails or high-risk features
Continue monitoring and review reversibility before permanent pacing
questions.explanation: Independent P waves and QRS complexes with a slow ventricular rate indicate complete heart block. In inferior MI the right coronary artery supplies the AV node in most people, so ischaemia of the node explains the block, and unstable bradycardia is treated with atropine then pacing.
